summary: Resolves inconsistent definitions and use of the GMPLS Switching Capability and Switching Type fields across technologies, by narrowly scoping what the fields mean. It is a clarification of existing definitions rather than a new technology.

eli5.summary: The same label meant different things in different places, so they cleaned up the meanings.

questions: what is the gmpls switching capability field
what is the gmpls switching type
which gmpls switching types are deprecated
subtitle: A narrow clean-up of what the GMPLS Switching Capability and Switching Type values are allowed to mean.

tldr.problem: GMPLS routing and signaling share one set of values for the type of switching, but the values were defined inconsistently across technologies, and some were of little value.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC narrows the fields: a different Switching Type SHOULD be used per data-plane technology, a different value MUST be used for each format of the Switching Capability-specific information, and PSC-2, PSC-3 and PSC-4 are deprecated.
tldr.outcome: No known deployments used the deprecated values, so there were no compatibility issues. The RFC updates RFC 3471, RFC 4202, RFC 4203 and RFC 5307.

today: RFC 7074 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3471, RFC 4202, RFC 4203 and RFC 5307.

sections.title: Why the Fields Needed Fixing
sections.content:
Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) controls several switching technologies, and hierarchical switching inside a technology. Routing protocols carry the kind of switching in the Switching Capability field, and signaling protocols carry it in the Switching Type field. The RFC calls the values in both fields Switching Types.

These values were not defined and used consistently across technologies. This document narrows what the fields mean and how they are used. It updates all documents that use the fields, in particular RFC 3471, RFC 4202, RFC 4203 and RFC 5307.
sections.eli5: Everyone used the same name tag but meant slightly different things by it. This document says exactly what the tag is for.

sections.title: How the Values Were Used Before
sections.content:
The original GMPLS architecture in RFC 3945 had five types of switching capability, and RFC 6002 added a sixth: Packet Switch Capable (PSC), Layer-2 Switch Capable (L2SC), Time-Division Multiplex Capable (TDM), Lambda Switch Capable (LSC), Fiber-Switch Capable (FSC) and Data Channel Switching Capable (DCSC). Each type had a single value, except PSC, which had four values (PSC-1 to PSC-4) to mark four levels of hierarchy.

A Switching Type did not name a specific data-plane technology. L2SC covered Ethernet and ATM, and TDM covered both SONET/SDH and G.709. The assumption was that different technologies of the same type would never run in the same signaling and routing domain.

That proved a problem for two reasons. Some technologies, such as Ethernet, have several levels of switching inside a provider network. And the routing Switching Capability value tells the IGP (the interior routing protocol) which format the Switching Capability-specific information (SCSI) field has, which is impractical to infer for implementations that support several technologies. This led to two new Ethernet types, EVPL in RFC 6004 and 802_1 PBB-TE in RFC 6060. The multiple PSC values had little value: there were no known uses of PSC-2, PSC-3 and PSC-4.
sections.eli5: Some labels were too broad, like calling every kind of road just a road, and some labels were never used at all.

sections.title: The Revised Definitions
sections.content:
For routing, the Switching Cap field indicates the type of switching being advertised via GMPLS Switching Type values. A different Switching Type value SHOULD be used for each data-plane technology, even when technologies share the same kind of multiplexing. For example, TDM technologies with different multiplexing structures, such as SDH and OTN, should use two different Switching Types.

Because the format of the SCSI field depends on this field, a different Switching Type value MUST be used to tell different SCSI formats apart. In practice, any time a new technology might use a different SCSI format, a new Switching Type SHOULD be used. The format of the Interface Switching Capability Descriptor itself is not changed.

For signaling, the Switching Type field indicates the type of switching to perform on a link, and it maps to one of the values advertised for that link in the routing Switching Capability Descriptor. The RFC notes that from a practical standpoint there is no change to this field.
sections.eli5: If two things need different instructions, they get different labels. The label on a signal still has to match a label the link already announced.

sections.title: Deprecated Switching Types
sections.content:
The RFC deprecates values 2, 3 and 4, which were Packet-Switch Capable-2 (PSC-2), PSC-3 and PSC-4. These values SHOULD be treated as unsupported types. In signaling they are processed according to Section 2.1.1 of RFC 3473.

In effect, the Switching Type is no longer an identifier of hierarchy levels within a technology. It is limited to identifying a per-technology SCSI field format.
sections.eli5: Three labels that nobody ever stuck on anything are taken off the shelf.

sections.title: Compatibility
sections.content: For existing implementations, the main impact is the deprecation of PSC-2, PSC-3 and PSC-4. At the time of publication there were no known deployments, or even implementations, that used these values, so the RFC reports no compatibility issues for current routing and signaling implementations.
sections.eli5: Since nobody was using the removed labels, nothing breaks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document changes the values carried in a single field in signaling and routing protocols. It defines no new protocol formats or mechanisms, so it raises no particular security implications. For general MPLS and GMPLS security issues the RFC points to the security framework in RFC 5920.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is built, so there is nothing new to worry about.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA has revised the Switching Types portion of the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry so that values 2, 3 and 4 read Deprecated and cite this document. Registration is by Standards Action. A parallel change was made to the IANA-GMPLS-TC-MIB, where psc2(2), psc3(3) and psc4(4) are marked deprecated.

The other assigned values are 1 (PSC-1), 30 (EVPL), 40 (802_1 PBB-TE), 51 (L2SC), 100 (TDM), 125 (DCSC), 150 (LSC) and 200 (FSC).
sections.eli5: The official list is updated to show the three removed labels as retired.
